donor_industry.caption: From itemized individual contributions over $200 reported to the FEC, grouped by the donor's self-reported employer and occupation. votes.question: On Passage — Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008)
votes.bill_title: Stop Insider Trading Act
votes.plain_language: This bill generally bars members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from buying stocks, and it requires public notice before they sell. A Yea passes it in the House. A Nay votes against passage.

votes.question: On Motion to Recommit — Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008)
votes.bill_title: Stop Insider Trading Act
votes.plain_language: The Stop Insider Trading Act would bar members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from buying stocks and would require public notice before a sale. This vote would have replaced that bill with a broader ban that also forces members, the President, the Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children to sell covered investments they already hold. A Yea would have made that swap; a Nay kept the original bill.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended — Combating Organized Retail Crime Act (H R 2853)
votes.bill_title: Combating Organized Retail Crime Act of 2025
votes.plain_language: This bill expands federal enforcement of criminal offenses related to organized retail and supply chain crime. This vote was under suspension of the rules, so a two-thirds vote was required. A Yea supports passing it as amended; a Nay opposes it.

votes.question: On Passage — Law-Enforcement Innovate to De-Escalate Act (H R 2189)
votes.bill_title: To modernize Federal firearms laws to account for advancements in technology and less-than-lethal weapons, and for other purposes.
votes.plain_language: This bill removes less-than-lethal projectile devices (e.g., certain TASERs) from regulation under the Gun Control Act. A Yea supports passing it in the House; a Nay opposes it.

It was great to join a pre-screening of the upcoming Madden film hosted by the Motion Picture Association, the NFL, and Amazon MGM Studios in Washington this week.

As I shared in my remarks, film and television production are important economic drivers in Pennsylvania and across America, bringing investment, creating jobs and driving tourism.

As Pennsylvania’s Secretary of Revenue, I fought to create a tax credit of up to 30% for film and television production that spends 60% of its budget in Pennsylvania. But we can still do more to bring these productions back to the United States, which is why I’m a cosponsor of the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, legislation that would establish a 20% federal tax credit for qualifying domestic film and television projects.

Films produced in Pennsylvania, like The Sixth Sense and Rocky, are more than just entertainment, they also shape our culture and encourage tourism.

Thank you to Motion Picture Association President and CEO Ambassador Charles Rivkin and NFL Vice President of Public Policy and Government Affairs, Brendon Plack, for bringing us together to celebrate a film about one of the most recognizable figures in American sports.

Today, I joined community leaders for the groundbreaking of the Coblentz Corner project in downtown Berwick.

I’m pleased to see the Coblentz Corner project breaking ground after years of preparation, coordination with state and local officials, and my office working to secure $1.5 million in federal funding to make this possible. The new Coblentz Corner facility will house a teen center, entrepreneurship academy, and restaurant incubator in the heart of Berwick.

This success demonstrates why community projects and constituent services are so important to me and my team. When we work with state and local leaders on these projects, relationships are enhanced, and we deliver strong results for residents and businesses. I’m pleased to have played a role in securing the funding for this transformation at the heart of Berwick and look forward to the many benefits it will have for the community once completed.

Thank you to Senator Lynda Culver and Representative Robert Ledbeter for supporting this project in the state legislature, and County Commissioners Dean Brewer, Randy Karschner, and David Kovach, Berwick Borough Manager Damien Scoblink, Deputy Director of Community Strategies Group Josh Nespoli, President of the Columbia-Montour Chamber of Commerce Chris Berleth, and For The Cause Teen Center for supporting this project.

roll_calls.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended — Ratepayer Protection Act (H R 9340)
roll_calls.plain_language: This bill tells state utility regulators to consider making very large power users, such as data centers using 100 megawatts or more, pay the full extra cost of grid upgrades built to serve them. A two-thirds vote was required. A Yea supports passing it as amended; a Nay opposes it.

financial_disclosures.caption: Official House financial disclosure filings from the Clerk of the House. A filing lists assets, income, liabilities, and trades the member reported; it is not proof of a conflict or of wrongdoing. Dollar ranges and asset names are in the PDF. This page links to the Clerk's copies and does not score anyone.

funding.heading: Disclosed campaign receipts
funding.detail: Federal cards show the principal campaign committee and OpenFEC totals for one two-year cycle, plus itemized Schedule A contributors. House uses 2026. Senate uses the cycle of the next election (2026, 2028, or 2030). This is not career fundraising and does not include Schedule E outside spending. Governors do not get a federal contribution list.

town_halls.note: There is no national town-hall dataset. Dates are not estimated.

disclosure_note: Disclosed contributions only; donors behind groups that do not report their own donors are not in this feed.
vote_scope: This is not a full career record. The cache is the latest 40 House rolls (2026, rolls 275-314) and 40 Senate votes (119th Congress, session 2, votes 217-256).
